claim: Feeding of 7 days old w;Hml-Gal4,UAS-2xeGFP/+ (Hml/+) flies with PQ-supplemented sucrose solution led to an increased lethality of adult Drosophila after 18 hr in a dose-dependent manner (0 mM: 1.25 ± 1.25%, 2 mM: 2.5 ± 1.64%, 15 mM: 27.78 ± 5.47%, and 30 mM: 38.75 ± 6.67%).
source: Feeding of 7 days old w;Hml-Gal4,UAS-2xeGFP/+ (Hml/+) flies with PQ-supplemented sucrose solution led to an increased lethality of adult Drosophila after 18 hr in a dose-dependent manner ( 0 mM: 1.25 ± 1.25%, 2 mM: 2.5 ± 1.6 4%, 15 mM: 27.78 ± 5.47%, and 30 mM: 38.75 ± 6.67%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PQ-feeding experiments with specific mortality percentages reported.

claim: 15 mM PQ was chosen for further experiments based on previous studies.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Wang et al., 2003), 15 mM PQ was chosen for further experiments (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2003 and experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PQ-induced damage of gut enterocytes and resulting gut leakage was not observed after 18 hr on 15 mM PQ food.
source: We tested if the death of flies after 18 hr on 15 mM PQ food was associated with PQ-induced damage of gut enterocytes and resulting gut leakage, but we found no indication of gut leakage on 15 mM PQ food (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from gut leakage assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only very few flies on control food and PQ indicated gut leakage of the food color to thorax and abdomen, which was unrelated to the treatment and not altered between the groups (control: 3.75%, 2 mM PQ: 2.53%, 15 mM PQ: 1.11% and 30 mM PQ: 3.75%).
source: Only very few flies on control food and PQ indicated gut leakage of the food color to thorax and abdomen, which was unrelated to the treatment and not altered between the groups (control: 3.75%, 2 mM PQ: 2.53 %, 15 mM PQ: 1.11% and 30 mM PQ: 3.75 %) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from gut leakage assays with specific percentages reported.

claim: Genes associated with carbohydrate metabolism such as insulin receptor (InR), phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (Pepck), and Thor were significantly upregulated upon PQ-feeding.
source: In contrast, genes associated with carbohydrate metabolism such as insulin receptor (InR), phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (Pepck), and Thor were significantly upregulated upon PQ-feeding (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The findings point to an activation of forkhead box, sub-group O (foxo)-target genes and a potentially reduced insulin signaling.
source: These findings point to an activation of forkhead box, sub-group O (foxo)-target genes and a potentially reduced insulin signaling, despite the lack of significant alterations in the expression of the Insulin-like peptides (Ilps) Ilp2, Ilp3, and Ilp5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression data and established knowledge about foxo-target genes.

claim: No significant alterations in the expression of the Insulin-like peptides (Ilps) Ilp2, Ilp3, and Ilp5 were observed upon PQ treatment.
source: These findings point to an activation of forkhead box, sub-group O (foxo)-target genes and a potentially reduced insulin signaling, despite the lack of significant alterations in the expression of the Insulin-like peptides (Ilps) Ilp2, Ilp3, and Ilp5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No changes in free glucose levels were found between control and PQ-treated flies (control: 1.49±0.02 µg and PQ: 1.50±0.07 µg, ns p=0.954).
source: Although no changes in free glucose levels (control: 1.49±0.02 µg and PQ: 1.50±0.07 µg, ns p=0.954) (Figure 1D) were found, we observed a clear decrease in stored glycogen (control: 1.02±0.07 µg and PQ: 0.33±0.08 µg, **p=0.003) (Figure 1E) and stored triglycerides (Figure 1F) in PQ-treated flies compared to control.
evidence: The claim is supported by glucose assay data with statistical analysis.

claim: A clear decrease in stored glycogen was observed in PQ-treated flies compared to control (control: 1.02±0.07 µg and PQ: 0.33±0.08 µg, **p=0.003).
source: Although no changes in free glucose levels (control: 1.49±0.02 µg and PQ: 1.50±0.07 µg, ns p=0.954) (Figure 1D) were found, we observed a clear decrease in stored glycogen (control: 1.02±0.07 µg and PQ: 0.33±0.08 µg, **p=0.003) (Figure 1E) and stored triglycerides (Figure 1F) in PQ-treated flies compared to control.
evidence: The claim is supported by glycogen assay data with statistical analysis.

claim: Stored triglycerides decreased in PQ-treated flies compared to control.
source: Although no changes in free glucose levels (control: 1.49±0.02 µg and PQ: 1.50±0.07 µg, ns p=0.954) (Figure 1D) were found, we observed a clear decrease in stored glycogen (control: 1.02±0.07 µg and PQ: 0.33±0.08 µg, **p=0.003) (Figure 1E) and stored triglycerides (Figure 1F) in PQ-treated flies compared to control.
evidence: The claim is supported by thin-layer chromatography data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: H&E and Oil Red O stainings showed a shrinkage in fat body cell size and stored lipid-filled vesicles in the abdominal fat body compared to flies kept under control conditions.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Oil Red O (ORO) stainings showed a shrinkage in fat body cell size and stored lipid-filled vesicles in the abdominal fat body compared to flies kept under control conditions Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No alterations in hemocyte numbers were observed after 18 hr on PQ or control food (control: 243.4±24.33 hemocytes per fly and PQ: 219.6±24.22 hemocytes per fly, ns p=0.508).
source: Our analysis did not reveal alterations in hemocyte numbers and especially no oxidative stress induced loss of hemocytes (control: 243.4±24.33 hemocytes per fly and PQ: 219.6±24.22 hemocytes per fly, ns p=0.508) (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by hemocyte quantification data with statistical analysis.

claim: Hemocyte-deficient flies displayed a significantly higher mortality rate on 15 mM PQ (43.33 ± 6.30%) compared to control flies (13.08 ± 2.63%).
source: Hemocyte-deficient flies displayed a significantly higher mortality rate on 15 mM PQ (43.33 ± 6.30%) compared to control flies (13.08 ± 2.63%) (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data comparing hemocyte-deficient and control flies.

claim: Hemocyte-deficient flies compared to the control genotype mobilized less triglycerides from the fat body during oxidative stress.
source: Interestingly, we found that hemocyte-deficient flies compared to the control genotype mobilized less triglycerides from the fat body during oxidative stress (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by thin-layer chromatography data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Hemocyte-deficient flies show a decrease in free glucose upon PQ feeding, whereas the control genotype showed similar free glucose levels as on normal food.
source: When we looked into free glucose levels, we found that these flies show a decrease in free glucose upon PQ feeding, whereas the control genotype showed similar free glucose levels as on normal food (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by glucose assay data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: No difference in glycogen levels was detected between the two genotypes on control food and on PQ food.
source: In contrast, we did not detect any difference in glycogen levels between the two genotypes on control food and on PQ food (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by glycogen assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: The presence or absence of hemocytes is a key determinant of the susceptibility to oxidative stress and results in altered energy mobilization in adult Drosophila.
source: Our findings show detrimental changes in energy mobilization upon oxidative stress in the absence of profound systemic overactivation of immune signaling cascades, however the presence or absence of hemocytes seem to be a key determinant of the susceptibility to oxidative stress and results in altered energy mobilization in adult Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including survival assays and metabolic measurements.

claim: Hemocytes play an essential role in controlling stress response and organismal survival upon oxidative stress.
source: This strongly points to an essential role for hemocytes in controlling stress response and organismal survival upon oxidative stress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing increased susceptibility of hemocyte-deficient flies.

claim: A total of 29,000 nuclei were obtained from two independent sorts for single nucleus RNA-sequencing.
source: From two independent sorts, we obtained a total of 29,000 nuclei, which were utilized for subsequent droplet-based barcoding of single nuclei, and generation of single nucleus cDNA libraries.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the snRNA-seq procedure.

claim: Gene expression data was successfully obtained from 11,839 nuclei.
source: We could successfully obtain gene expression data from 11,839 nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of all analyzed nuclei revealed 20 distinct nuclei clusters with differential gene expression.
source: Quality control analysis followed by unsupervised hierarchical clustering of all analyzed nuclei using Seurat package (Hao et al., 2021) revealed 20 distinct nuclei clusters (C) with differential gene expression (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of snRNA-seq data using the Seurat package.

claim: All annotated cell types were detected in PQ-treated and control flies.
source: All annotated cell types were detected in PQ-treated and control flies (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Three of the clusters were annotated as hemocytes (clusters: 2, 11, and 14).
source: Using cell type-specific signatures, three of the clusters were annotated as hemocytes (clusters: 2, 11, and 14; Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell type annotation based on known signatures.

claim: Re-scaling and clustering of all 1354 identified hemocyte nuclei revealed 8 distinct clusters.
source: Re-scaling and clustering of all 1354 identified hemocyte nuclei revealed 8 distinct clusters (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of hemocyte-specific snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster 8 expressed various crystal cell-specific markers including lozenge (lz), pebbled (peb), prophenoloxidase 1 (PPO1), and prophenoloxidase 2 (PPO2).
source: Cluster 8 expressed various crystal cell-specific markers including lozenge (lz), pebbled (peb), prophenoloxidase 1 (PPO1), and prophenoloxidase 2 (PPO2), whereas all other clusters seemed to be plasmatocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: All clusters except cluster 8 seemed to be plasmatocytes.
source: Cluster 8 expressed various crystal cell-specific markers including lozenge (lz), pebbled (peb), prophenoloxidase 1 (PPO1), and prophenoloxidase 2 (PPO2), whereas all other clusters seemed to be plasmatocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–L).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns and known cell type markers.

claim: The embryonic and larval hemocyte markers Hemese (He) and singed (sn) were not expressed across any of the identified clusters.
source: In line with previous reports, the embryonic and larval hemocyte markers Hemese (He) (data not shown) and singed (sn) were not expressed across any of the identified clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data and previous reports.

claim: The two plasmatocyte clusters C1 and C7 were primarily derived from control flies.
source: Interestingly, when we defined which hemocyte clusters were enriched in control flies or PQ-treated flies, the two plasmatocyte clusters C1 and C7 were primarily derived from control flies, whereas C2, C3, C4, and C6 are predominantly found in PQ-treated flies (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis showing cluster distribution by treatment condition.

claim: Clusters C2, C3, C4, and C6 are predominantly found in PQ-treated flies.
source: Interestingly, when we defined which hemocyte clusters were enriched in control flies or PQ-treated flies, the two plasmatocyte clusters C1 and C7 were primarily derived from control flies, whereas C2, C3, C4, and C6 are predominantly found in PQ-treated flies (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis showing cluster distribution by treatment condition.

claim: The plasmatocyte cluster C5 and the crystal cell cluster C8 presented in both conditions to similar proportions.
source: The plasmatocyte cluster C5 as well as the crystal cell cluster C8 presented in both conditions to similar proportions (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis showing cluster distribution by treatment condition.

claim: Plasmatocyte cluster C1 had a remarkable expression of hemocyte specific marker genes such as Hml and Pxn, as well as migration-associated genes including the semaphorins Sema2a and Sema5c.
source: Plasmatocyte cluster C1, which was mostly present in control conditions, had a remarkable expression of hemocyte specific marker genes such as Hml and Pxn, as well as migration-associated genes including the semaphorins Sema2a and Sema5c (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C1 showed higher expression of genes contributing to metabolic regulations such as the L-gulonate 3-dehydrogenase Had2 and the gluconolactonase regucalcin.
source: Yet this cluster also showed higher expression of genes contributing to metabolic regulations such as the L-gulonate 3-dehydrogenase Had2 and the gluconolactonase regucalcin (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C7 and C1 substantially shared gene expression profiles.
source: The cluster C7 and C1, mostly found in control flies, substantially shared gene expression profiles.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of gene expression patterns from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C2 and C3 were nearly exclusively found in PQ-treated flies and showed expression of genes involved in metabolic adaptations.
source: In contrast, cluster C2 and C3 were nearly exclusively found in PQ-treated flies and showed expression of genes involved in metabolic adaptations.
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis showing cluster distribution and gene expression patterns.

claim: Metabolic adaptation within cluster C2 included high expression of the glucose transporter 4 enhancer factor (Glut4EF) and the phosphatidate phosphatase Lipin (Lpin).
source: Metabolic adaptation within these clusters included high expression of the glucose transporter 4 enhancer factor (Glut4EF) and the phosphatidate phosphatase Lipin (Lpin) in C2 or the induced expression of the lipase brummer (bmm), the autophagy-associated gene-17 (Atg17) or the lipophorin receptor 1 (LpR1), involved in uptake of neutral lipids from the hemolymph, in C3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C3 showed induced expression of the lipase brummer (bmm), the autophagy-associated gene-17 (Atg17) and the lipophorin receptor 1 (LpR1).
source: Metabolic adaptation within these clusters included high expression of the glucose transporter 4 enhancer factor (Glut4EF) and the phosphatidate phosphatase Lipin (Lpin) in C2 or the induced expression of the lipase brummer (bmm), the autophagy-associated gene-17 (Atg17) or the lipophorin receptor 1 (LpR1), involved in uptake of neutral lipids from the hemolymph, in C3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Overall gene expression profiles in clusters C2 and C3 showed an induction of insulin signaling, increased autophagy and lipolysis pointing to adaptation of energy mobilization in these clusters upon PQ treatment.
source: Overall gene expression profiles in clusters C2 and C3 showed an induction of insulin signaling, increased autophagy and lipolysis pointing to adaptation of energy mobilization in these clusters upon PQ treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns related to metabolic pathways.

claim: Cluster C4 was characterized by a remarkable upregulation of genes involved in translation including many ribosomal proteins such as RpL8, RpL31, or RpS13.
source: Cluster C4 was characterized by a remarkable upregulation of genes involved in translation including many ribosomal proteins such as RpL8, RpL31, or RpS13 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C4 included genes associated with unsaturated fatty acid metabolism such as Desaturase 1 (Desat1).
source: Furthermore, C4 included genes associated with unsaturated fatty acid metabolism such as Desaturase 1 (Desat1).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C5 showed induction of genes involved in fatty acid metabolism such as ELOVL fatty acid elongase 7 (ELOVL).
source: Similarly, cluster C5 also showed induction of genes involved in fatty acid metabolism such as ELOVL fatty acid elongase 7 (ELOVL) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Tie-like receptor tyrosine kinase (Tie) was specifically expressed in cluster C5.
source: Of note, we also found Tie-like receptor tyrosine kinase (Tie) specifically expressed in this cluster, which is described to bind PDGF- and VEGF-related factor (Pvf) ligands and contribute to cell survival and migration, as well as actin-associated binding proteins including polychaetoid (pyd) and formin 3 (form3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data and established knowledge about Tie function.

claim: Cluster C6 presented a strong immune activation phenotype with induction of Jak/STAT target genes including Fasciclin 3 (Fas3) and Turandot-M (TotM).
source: Among all plasmatocyte clusters, we found cluster C6 which presented a strong immune activation phenotype with induction of Jak/STAT target genes including Fasciclin 3 (Fas3) and Turandot-M (TotM) among its TOP20 DE genes, but also activation of oxidative stress response genes such as the heat shock proteins Hsp23, Hsp26 and Hsp27 or cytoskeletal genes including myosin Myo31DF or spire (spir) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C6 showed activation of oxidative stress response genes such as the heat shock proteins Hsp23, Hsp26 and Hsp27.
source: Among all plasmatocyte clusters, we found cluster C6 which presented a strong immune activation phenotype with induction of Jak/STAT target genes including Fasciclin 3 (Fas3) and Turandot-M (TotM) among its TOP20 DE genes, but also activation of oxidative stress response genes such as the heat shock proteins Hsp23, Hsp26 and Hsp27 or cytoskeletal genes including myosin Myo31DF or spire (spir) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C6 showed expression of cytoskeletal genes including myosin Myo31DF or spire (spir).
source: Among all plasmatocyte clusters, we found cluster C6 which presented a strong immune activation phenotype with induction of Jak/STAT target genes including Fasciclin 3 (Fas3) and Turandot-M (TotM) among its TOP20 DE genes, but also activation of oxidative stress response genes such as the heat shock proteins Hsp23, Hsp26 and Hsp27 or cytoskeletal genes including myosin Myo31DF or spire (spir) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C1 showed that Sema2a seems to be exceptionally high expressed in homeostatic plasmatocytes.
source: However, cluster C1 showed that Sema2a seems to be exceptionally high expressed in these homeostatic plasmatocytes and genes associated with metabolic regulation (e.g. InR, Lpin or bmm) or Jak/STAT activation (e.g. Fas3), as seen in PQ-associated clusters, are downregulated (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C5 showed enrichment for genes such as the transcription factor grainy head (grh) and cytoskeletal-associated genes such as jitterbug (jbug) and form3.
source: Cluster C5 showed enrichment for genes such as the transcription factor grainy head (grh) but also cytoskeletal-associated genes such as jitterbug (jbug) and form3, suggesting a migratory potential of plasmatocytes from this cluster within their host tissues (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Plasmatocyte cluster C6 presented with the most profound gene expression changes compared to all other clusters.
source: Interestingly, plasmatocyte cluster C6 presented with the most profound gene expression changes compared to all other clusters.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of differential gene expression across clusters.

claim: Genes specifically expressed in cluster C6 were associated with Jak/STAT pathway activation (e.g. Fas3, TotM), cytoskeletal rearrangements and migration (e.g. Myo31DF, spir or cheerio [cher]) and response to oxidative stress (e.g. Nicotinamide amidase [Naam] or Hsp23).
source: Similar to our previous observations, we identified that genes specifically expressed in this cluster were associated with Jak/STAT pathway activation (e.g. Fas3, TotM), cytoskeletal rearrangements and migration (e.g. Myo31DF, spir or cheerio [cher]) and response to oxidative stress (e.g. Nicotinamide amidase [Naam] or Hsp23; Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Adult hemocytes respond differentially to oxidative stress with a specific cluster of plasmatocytes associated with immune activation and stress response.
source: Our snRNA-seq analysis revealed that adult hemocytes respond differentially to oxidative stress with a specific cluster of plasmatocytes associated with immune activation and stress response.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comprehensive snRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Plasmatocyte cluster C6 showed a substantial immune response toward oxidative stress.
source: Despite our findings that on systemic level we did not detect a strong induction of immune activation upon oxidative stress, we now provide evidence that plasmatocyte cluster C6 showed a substantial immune response toward oxidative stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: S2 cells showed a dose-dependent increase in intracellular ROS at all time points analyzed with higher ROS levels at 6 hr (0 mM: 1903±64 MFI, 15 mM: 6735±1,096 MFI, and 30 mM: 7435±237 MFI) compared to 24 hr (0 mM: 1236±135 MFI, 15 mM: 4456±228 MFI, and 30 mM: 5557±303 MFI).
source: We observed a dose-dependent increase in intracellular ROS at all time points analyzed with higher ROS levels at 6 hr (0 mM: 1903±64 median fluorescence intensity (MFI), 15 mM: 6735±1,096 MFI, and 30 mM: 7435±237 MFI) compared to 24 hr (0 mM: 1236±135 MFI, 15 mM: 4456±228 MFI, and 30 mM: 5557±303 MFI; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring ROS levels in S2 cells.

claim: Upon PQ treatment, S2 cells showed a remarkable and dose-dependent increase in DNA damage compared to untreated cells (0 mM: 101.0±2.1, 5 mM: 117.6±3.3, 10 mM: 136.6±3.8, and 15 mM: 147.8±5.5, data shown as olive tail moment).
source: Upon PQ treatment, S2 cells showed a remarkable and dose-dependent increase in DNA damage compared to untreated cells (0 mM: 101.0±2.1, 5 mM: 117.6±3.3, 10 mM: 136.6±3.8, and 15 mM: 147.8±5.5, data shown as olive tail moment; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comet assay data measuring DNA damage in S2 cells.

claim: Direct exposure of S2 cells with PQ in vitro mimics gene expression changes seen in a particular activated cell stage of plasmatocytes upon oxidative stress in vivo.
source: All these results further support our hypothesis that direct exposure of S2 cells with PQ in vitro mimics gene expression changes seen in a particular activated cell stage of plasmatocytes upon oxidative stress in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing in vitro and in vivo gene expression data.

claim: A slight, but significant, induction of the cytokine daw was identified in PQ-treated S2 cells.
source: We identified a slight, but significant, induction of the cytokine daw, but no other alterations in dpp or the AMPs Drs, Dro, or Mtk (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from PQ-treated S2 cells.

claim: No alterations in dpp or the AMPs Drs, Dro, or Mtk were observed in PQ-treated S2 cells.
source: We identified a slight, but significant, induction of the cytokine daw, but no other alterations in dpp or the AMPs Drs, Dro, or Mtk (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from PQ-treated S2 cells.

claim: Cluster C6 plasmatocytes reflect a cellular state associated with the direct response to oxidative stress in vivo.
source: The profound induction of Jak/STAT target genes together with the activation of JNK target genes and oxidative stress induced DNA damage in S2 cells in vitro highly support our hypothesis that cluster C6 plasmatocytes reflect a cellular state associated with the direct response to oxidative stress in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing in vitro S2 cell data with in vivo snRNA-seq data.

claim: An enriched expression of Jak/STAT target genes (upd3, Socs36E, TotA, TotM, and Fas3) was identified in cluster C6.
source: Here, we identified an enriched expression of these genes in cluster C6, and a unique expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine upd3 in cluster C6, which was not detected in any other hemocyte cluster (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: A unique expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine upd3 was found in cluster C6, which was not detected in any other hemocyte cluster.
source: Here, we identified an enriched expression of these genes in cluster C6, and a unique expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine upd3 in cluster C6, which was not detected in any other hemocyte cluster (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible 45 (Gadd45) was enriched in plasmatocyte cluster C6.
source: Interestingly, we also identified that Growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible 45 (Gadd45), a gene linking DNA damage signaling and stress induced JNK signaling, was enriched in plasmatocyte cluster C6 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Gadd45 is a gene linking DNA damage signaling and stress induced JNK signaling.
source: Interestingly, we also identified that Growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible 45 (Gadd45), a gene linking DNA damage signaling and stress induced JNK signaling, was enriched in plasmatocyte cluster C6 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Gadd45 function.

claim: The JNK target gene puc was expressed across all hemocyte clusters analyzed in vivo without a specific induction in cluster C6.
source: However within our snRNA-seq analysis, the JNK target gene puc was expressed across all hemocyte clusters analyzed in vivo without a specific induction in cluster C6 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C6 plasmatocytes represent a functional state of activated plasmatocytes directly responding to oxidative stress by JNK signaling and Jak/STAT pathway activation.
source: These findings from the snRNA-seq analysis in vivo and S2 cells in vitro support the hypothesis that cluster C6 plasmatocytes represent a functional state of activated plasmatocytes directly responding to oxidative stress by JNK signaling and Jak/STAT pathway activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Cluster C6 specifically expresses the cytokine upd3, which could reflect an important mediator for oxidative stress response.
source: Furthermore, we found evidence that cluster C6 specifically expresses the cytokine upd3, which could reflect an important mediator for oxidative stress response.
evidence: The claim is based on gene expression data and speculation about functional significance.

claim: Re-scaling and clustering of all 3150 identified fat body nuclei revealed 8 distinct clusters.
source: Re-scaling and clustering of all 3150 identified fat body nuclei revealed 8 distinct clusters (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of fat body-specific snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C1, C6 and C8 were mainly enriched with fat body cells obtained from control flies.
source: From the eight distinct fat body cell clusters, we identified that cluster C1, C6 and C8 were mainly enriched with cells obtained from control flies, whereas clusters C2-5 were almost exclusively derived from PQ-treated flies (Figure 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis showing cluster distribution by treatment condition.

claim: Clusters C2-5 were almost exclusively derived from PQ-treated flies.
source: From the eight distinct fat body cell clusters, we identified that cluster C1, C6 and C8 were mainly enriched with cells obtained from control flies, whereas clusters C2-5 were almost exclusively derived from PQ-treated flies (Figure 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis showing cluster distribution by treatment condition.

claim: Only cluster C7 represents fat body cells from both conditions.
source: Only cluster C7 represents cells from both conditions (Figure 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by snRNA-seq data analysis showing cluster distribution by treatment condition.

claim: Fat body cluster C1 showed an enrichment for gene induction associated with triglyceride storage, such as Fatty acid synthase 1 (FASN1), Glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase 1 (Gpdh1) or Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain (Acsl).
source: Here the cluster C1, mostly derived of fat body cells from control flies, showed an enrichment for gene induction associated with triglyceride storage, such as Fatty acid synthase 1 (FASN1), Glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase 1 (Gpdh1) or Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain (Acsl), as well as fat body signature genes (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cluster C8 showed a distinct expression of AMP genes including Dro, Drs or Diptericin-B (DptB), however this cluster completely disappeared after PQ feeding.
source: Interestingly cluster C8, which mostly consisted of cells from control food, showed a distinct expression of AMP genes including Dro, Drs or Diptericin-B (DptB), however this cluster completely disappeared after PQ feeding (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis and cluster distribution data from snRNA-seq.

claim: Cluster C2, C4, and C5 showed a strong gene induction of oxidative stress response genes, but also genes associated with Jak/STAT pathway (e.g. Socs36E, upd3, Fas3, TotA) and JNK activation (e.g. puc, kay).
source: For example, cluster C2, C4, and C5 showed a strong gene induction of oxidative stress response genes, but also genes associated with Jak/STAT pathway (e.g. Socs36E, upd3, Fas3, TotA) and JNK activation (e.g. puc, kay) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: In clusters C2, C4, and C5, genes associated with triglyceride storage were significantly reduced.
source: In all of these clusters, genes associated with triglyceride storage were significantly reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: The fat body has a unique heterogeneity upon oxidative stress with a clear separation of clusters with JNK and Jak/STAT activation signature.
source: Overall, our data revealed that the fat body has a unique heterogeneity upon oxidative stress with a clear separation of clusters with JNK and Jak/STAT activation signature, which could be either activated by the PQ-induced oxidative stress itself or by the cytokines released by immune-activated hemocytes, especially upd3.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from snRNA-seq data analysis of fat body cells.

claim: DDR-deficient flies (Hml >mei-41-IR, Hml >tefu-IR, Hml >mei41 IR;tefu-IR and Hml >nbs-IR) showed significantly increased susceptibility to PQ treatment compared to control genotype (Hml/+: 10.7 ± 1.2%, Hml >mei-41-IR: 40.7 ± 4.8%, Hml >tefu-IR: 20.7 ± 4.3%, Hml >mei41 IR;tefu-IR: 37.5 ± 4.8% and Hml >nbs-IR: 48.2 ± 6.7%).
source: We compared their susceptibility to PQ treatment after 18 hr and found significantly increased susceptibility to the treatment across all DDR-deficient lines compared to the control genotype (Hml/+: 10.7 ± 1.2%, Hml >mei-41-IR: 40.7 ± 4.8%, Hml >tefu-IR: 20.7 ± 4.3%, Hml >mei41 IR;tefu-IR: 37.5 ± 4.8% and Hml >nbs-IR: 48.2 ± 6.7%) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data comparing DDR-deficient and control flies.

claim: Decreased survival after PQ in DDR-deficient flies did not correlate to an overall reduction in lifespan on normal food and a decrease in fitness.
source: In these flies, decreased survival after PQ did not correlate to an overall reduction in lifespan on normal food and a decrease in fitness (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DDR-deficient flies did not show a decreased survival on starvation compared to the control genotype.
source: Importantly, we did not observe a decreased survival of DDR-deficient flies on starvation compared to the control genotype, indicating that the observed susceptibility to oxidative stress of flies with a DDR-deficiency in hemocytes is specifically caused by oxidative stress due to PQ treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by starvation survival assay data.

claim: The observed susceptibility to oxidative stress of flies with a DDR-deficiency in hemocytes is specifically caused by oxidative stress due to PQ treatment.
source: Importantly, we did not observe a decreased survival of DDR-deficient flies on starvation compared to the control genotype, indicating that the observed susceptibility to oxidative stress of flies with a DDR-deficiency in hemocytes is specifically caused by oxidative stress due to PQ treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing survival under different stress conditions.

claim: Temperature-inducible knock-down of mei-41, tefu and nbs1 in adult hemocytes resulted in higher susceptibility to oxidative stress compared to control (Hml-Gal80ts/+: 30.3 ± 5.2%, Hml-Gal80ts>mei-41-IR: 36.2 ± 4.3%, Hml-Gal80ts>tefu-IR: 52.4 ± 6.9%, Hml-Gal80ts>mei-41-IR;tefu-IR: 72.3 ± 6.3% and Hml-Gal80ts>nbs-IR: 36.2 ± 4.3%).
source: In contrast, we again found a higher susceptibility to oxidative stress via PQ-feeding in the DDR-deficient lines compared to control (Hml-Gal80ts/+: 30.3 ± 5.2%, Hml-Gal80ts>mei-41-IR: 36.2 ± 4.3%, Hml-Gal80ts>tefu-IR: 52.4 ± 6.9%, Hml-Gal80ts>mei-41-IR;tefu-IR: 72.3 ± 6.3% and Hml-Gal80ts>nbs-IR: 36.2 ± 4.3%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), which directly confirms our previous results and conclusions (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data using temperature-inducible knockdown system.

claim: No alteration in hemocyte number was found across all DDR-deficient fly lines on control food (with the exception of an increase in hemocytes in the Hml>tefu-IR line).
source: We did not find alteration in hemocyte number across all fly lines on control food (with the exception of an increase in hemocytes in the Hml>tefu-IR line), nor did we observe any effect of PQ treatment on the number of hemocytes in DDR-deficient flies (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hemocyte quantification data.

claim: No effect of PQ treatment on the number of hemocytes in DDR-deficient flies was observed.
source: We did not find alteration in hemocyte number across all fly lines on control food (with the exception of an increase in hemocytes in the Hml>tefu-IR line), nor did we observe any effect of PQ treatment on the number of hemocytes in DDR-deficient flies (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hemocyte quantification data.

claim: Comet assays of isolated hemocytes from DDR-deficient flies indicated only a slight increase in DNA damage.
source: Comet assays of isolated hemocytes from DDR-deficient flies and the control genotype on PQ and control food only indicated a slight increase in DNA damage in these flies, which demonstrates that the higher susceptibility of DDR-deficient flies is not due to a loss of hemocyte numbers or a substantial increase in DNA damage, but rather due to changes in the downstream DDR-signaling events modulating immune activation of hemocytes (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comet assay data measuring DNA damage.

claim: The higher susceptibility of DDR-deficient flies is not due to a loss of hemocyte numbers or a substantial increase in DNA damage, but rather due to changes in the downstream DDR-signaling events modulating immune activation of hemocytes.
source: Comet assays of isolated hemocytes from DDR-deficient flies and the control genotype on PQ and control food only indicated a slight increase in DNA damage in these flies, which demonstrates that the higher susceptibility of DDR-deficient flies is not due to a loss of hemocyte numbers or a substantial increase in DNA damage, but rather due to changes in the downstream DDR-signaling events modulating immune activation of hemocytes (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including hemocyte counts and DNA damage measurements.

claim: Loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes induced a significant induction of upd3 expression upon PQ treatment in Hml>tefu-IR and Hml>mei-41-IR;tefu-IR flies.
source: Loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes induced a significant induction of upd3 expression upon PQ treatment in Hml>tefu-IR and Hml>mei-41-IR;tefu-IR flies (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from DDR-deficient flies.

claim: upd1 and upd2 were not significantly changed in DDR-deficient flies.
source: In contrary, upd1 and upd2 were not significantly changed in DDR-deficient flies (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from DDR-deficient flies.

claim: A slight induction of Socs36E expression was observed in all DDR-deficient genotypes on PQ, but only Hml>mei-41-IR;tefu-IR flies showed a significant induction of Socs36E upon PQ treatment compared to control food and Hml/+ flies on PQ.
source: A slight induction of Socs36E expression in all DDR-deficient genotypes on PQ, but only Hml>mei-41-IR;tefu-IR flies showed a significant induction of Socs36E upon PQ treatment compared to control food and Hml/+ flies on PQ (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from DDR-deficient flies.

claim: A significant induction of puc was found on PQ treatment in Hml >tefu IR, Hml >mei-41-IR;tefu-IR and Hml >nbs IR flies, which was not seen in control flies upon PQ treatment.
source: However, when we checked the levels of puc, as a JNK signaling target gene, we found a significant induction on PQ treatment in Hml >tefu IR, Hml >mei-41-IR;tefu-IR and Hml >nbs IR flies, which was not seen in control flies upon PQ treatment (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from DDR-deficient flies.

claim: A significant induction and dysregulation of Thor and InR was detected in all DDR-deficient genotypes upon PQ treatment compared to control flies.
source: When we analyzed the gene expression of genes involved in metabolism and energy mobilization, we detected a significant induction and dysregulation of Thor and InR in all DDR-deficient genotypes upon PQ treatment compared to control flies (Figure 5E), as well as a slight induction of Pepck1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from DDR-deficient flies.

claim: Efficient mobilization of triglyceride storage upon PQ treatment was found in all genotypes compared to control food.
source: To further exclude that the higher susceptibility of DDR-deficient flies and seen alterations in stress response are due to inefficient mobilization of triglycerides, we measured stored triglycerides across all genotypes and found efficient mobilization of triglyceride storage upon PQ treatment in all genotypes compared to control food (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by thin-layer chromatography data.

claim: DNA damage signaling in adult hemocytes essentially determines susceptibility to oxidative stress.
source: From our results, we can conclude that DNA damage signaling in adult hemocytes, mostly consisting of plasmatocytes, essentially determines susceptibility to oxidative stress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results with DDR-deficient flies.

claim: Loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes results in upregulation of JNK signaling and elevated expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine upd3, as well as transcriptional alterations in energy mobilization and insulin signaling.
source: Loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes results in upregulation of JNK signaling and elevated expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine upd3, as well as transcriptional alterations in energy mobilization and insulin signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple gene expression analyses from DDR-deficient flies.

claim: The DNA damage signaling machinery in hemocytes is activated by oxidative stress and plays an essential modulatory and rate-limiting role for subsequent immune activation.
source: Based on our previous results on the role of hemocytes during oxidative stress, we can therefore assume that the DNA damage signaling machinery in hemocytes is activated by oxidative stress and plays an essential modulatory and rate-limiting role for subsequent immune activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results with DDR-deficient flies and oxidative stress treatments.

claim: Hml>upd3 flies showed a drastically decreased survival on PQ.
source: Both genotypes showed a normal overall lifespan compared to the Hml/+ control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), but when we compared their susceptibility to PQ-induced oxidative stress, Hml>upd3 flies showed a drastically decreased survival on PQ, whereas Hml>upd3 IR flies did not show a changed survival on PQ treatment after 18 hr (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data comparing upd3 overexpression and knockdown flies.

claim: Hml>upd3 IR flies did not show a changed survival on PQ treatment after 18 hr.
source: Both genotypes showed a normal overall lifespan compared to the Hml/+ control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), but when we compared their susceptibility to PQ-induced oxidative stress, Hml>upd3 flies showed a drastically decreased survival on PQ, whereas Hml>upd3 IR flies did not show a changed survival on PQ treatment after 18 hr (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data.

claim: Hml>upd3 flies showed increased levels of upd3 in both treatment groups compared to the other genotypes.
source: As expected, Hml>upd3 flies showed increased levels of upd3 in both treatment groups compared to the other genotypes, but also showed a significant increase of upd3 upon PQ compared to control food (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data measuring upd3 expression.

claim: upd3-null mutants had a significant reduced susceptibility to oxidative stress compared to Hml/+ flies.
source: Of note, we found that upd3null mutants had a significant reduced susceptibility to oxidative stress compared to Hml/+ flies, however we found a decreased survival in upd3null;Hml>upd3 flies when hemocytes alone overexpressing upd3 similar to the higher susceptibility of Hml>upd3 flies (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data comparing upd3-null mutants to control flies.

claim: upd3null;Hml>upd3 flies showed decreased survival similar to the higher susceptibility of Hml>upd3 flies.
source: Of note, we found that upd3null mutants had a significant reduced susceptibility to oxidative stress compared to Hml/+ flies, however we found a decreased survival in upd3null;Hml>upd3 flies when hemocytes alone overexpressing upd3 similar to the higher susceptibility of Hml>upd3 flies (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data.

claim: Loss of upd3 rescued the higher susceptibility of flies with DDR-deficient hemocytes.
source: Indeed, we found a substantially decreased susceptibility of these flies to oxidative stress compared to Hml>mei41-IR;tefu-IR flies, supporting our hypothesis that loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes and subsequently increased levels of upd3 render adult flies more susceptible to oxidative stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data comparing upd3null;Hml>mei41-IR;tefu-IR to Hml>mei41-IR;tefu-IR flies.

claim: Loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes and subsequently increased levels of upd3 render adult flies more susceptible to oxidative stress.
source: Indeed, we found a substantially decreased susceptibility of these flies to oxidative stress compared to Hml>mei41-IR;tefu-IR flies, supporting our hypothesis that loss of DNA damage signaling in hemocytes and subsequently increased levels of upd3 render adult flies more susceptible to oxidative stress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic rescue experiments.

claim: An increased susceptibility of Hml>hep[act] flies to PQ treatment was found.
source: We compared their survival on PQ after 18 hr and in line with our previous results, we found an increased susceptibility of Hml>hep[act] flies to PQ treatment, but not of Hml>bsk-DN flies compared to the control genotype (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data with JNK pathway manipulation.

claim: Hml>bsk-DN flies did not show increased susceptibility to PQ treatment compared to the control genotype.
source: We compared their survival on PQ after 18 hr and in line with our previous results, we found an increased susceptibility of Hml>hep[act] flies to PQ treatment, but not of Hml>bsk-DN flies compared to the control genotype (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data.

claim: A significant induction of upd3 expression after PQ treatment was found in Hml>hep[act] compared to control food.
source: Furthermore, when we analyzed upd3 expression in these flies upon PQ treatment, we found a significant induction of upd3 expression after PQ treatment in Hml>hep[act] compared to control food, but only a slight increase in Hml/+ and Hml>bsk-DN flies upon PQ feeding (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data measuring upd3 expression.

claim: JNK-mediated induction of upd3 in hemocytes plays a substantial role upon oxidative stress.
source: These findings support a substantial role of JNK-mediated induction of upd3 in hemocytes upon oxidative stress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from JNK pathway manipulation experiments.

claim: A defined immune-responsive subset of plasmatocytes exists during oxidative stress.
source: In summary, our study revealed a defined immune-responsive subset of plasmatocytes during oxidative stress.
evidence: The claim is based on comprehensive snRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Oxidative stress-mediated immune activation is regulated by DNA damage signaling in hemocytes, which controls JNK activation and subsequent upd3 expression.
source: We show that this oxidative stress-mediated immune activation seems to be regulated by DNA damage signaling in hemocytes, which controls JNK activation and subsequent upd3 expression (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including DDR-deficient flies and pathway manipulation.

claim: Loss of DNA damage signaling and over-induction of JNK signaling or upd3 in hemocytes renders the adult fly more susceptible to oxidative stress.
source: Loss of DNA damage signaling and over-induction of JNK signaling or upd3 in hemocytes release renders the adult fly more susceptible to oxidative stress (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple genetic manipulation experiments.
